issues.legal_issue: An application to restore property or money taken under a decree later reversed is an application for execution of the appellate decree.
material_facts: Property and costs had been obtained under a trial decree while an appeal was pending.
The appellate court reversed the trial decree, and the applicants sought restitution of the property and costs under the resulting decree.
The appellate decree was later amended, and the restitution application was filed within three years of that amendment.
issues.conclusion: The restitution application was an application for execution and was within time under Article 182 of the Limitation Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, restitution works out the benefit of the appellate decree and is an execution application, including where the appellate decree does not expressly direct restitution. The Court relied on the history of Section 144 and its predecessor, Section 583 of the 1882 Code; the principle in Jai Berham v. Kedar Nath Marwari that a court must restore parties to the position they would have occupied absent the varied or reversed decree; and the treatment of restitution as execution in Prag Narain Kamakhia Singh and the cited High Court authorities. Sections 37 and 38 support execution in the court of first instance, while Sections 47 and 144 must be read consistently. Article 182, rather than residuary Article 181, therefore governs limitation.

predicates.restitution_proceeding_after_reversal: A party applies for restitution after a decree under which the opposing party obtained a benefit has been reversed or varied.
predicates.property_or_money_taken_under_reversed_d: The opposing party obtained property or money by acting on the decree that was later reversed or varied.
predicates.application_seeks_restore_prior_position: The applicant seeks to restore the position that would have existed without the reversed or varied decree.
predicates.application_filed_within_three_years_of_: The restitution application is filed within three years after the appellate decree is amended.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to recover a benefit obtained under a reversed or varied decree, and applies within three years of an amendment to the appellate decree, the application is treated as execution and is within time.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial amendment to a decree that changes the parties’ rights starts a new limitation period for an execution application.
material_facts: An execution application sought recovery of costs awarded by the appellate decree.
The appellate decree was amended by deleting one of the persons in whose favour it had originally been made.
That deletion changed the rights of the parties under the decree, and the execution application was filed within three years of the amendment.
issues.conclusion: The amendment affected the parties’ rights and the execution application for costs was within time under Article 182(4) of the Limitation Act.
issues.legal_principle: Article 182(4) of the Limitation Act provides that the limitation period for executing an amended decree runs from the date of amendment. The Court held that deleting a person from the decree was a substantial amendment because it modified the parties’ rights; it was therefore unnecessary to decide whether a merely clerical correction would qualify.

predicates.costs_execution_proceeding: A party applies to execute a decree to recover costs awarded under it.
predicates.decree_amendment_changes_parties_rights: The decree is amended in a way that changes the rights of the parties under it.
predicates.application_filed_within_three_years_of_: The execution application is filed within three years after the decree is amended.

issues.definition: When an execution application seeks awarded costs, the decree has been amended to change the parties’ rights, and the application is filed within three years of that amendment, the application is within time.
